cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Imagine sending a small pulse along a stretched rope.
The pulse travels toward your friend, but a little mark on the rope moves up
and down, not all the way to your friend.
That's our first distinction: the disturbance travels while the material
oscillates locally.
Mechanical waves need a medium.
In a transverse wave, particle motion is perpendicular to propagation.
In a longitudinal wave, such as sound in air, it is parallel, producing
compressions and rarefactions.
For a sinusoidal wave, wavelength is the spacing between neighboring points
with the same phase, such as two crests.
Frequency counts oscillations per second.
In one period the pattern advances one wavelength, so wave speed equals
frequency times wavelength.
We can write displacement as amplitude times sine of k x minus omega t plus
phase.
Here k equals two pi divided by wavelength, and omega equals two pi times
frequency.
Holding phase constant shows that this minus sign form travels in the positive
x direction.
With a plus sign before omega t, it travels in the negative direction.
Take wavelength half a meter and frequency forty hertz.
The pattern moves at twenty meters per second.
That is not the speed of a marked particle.
Particle velocity comes from differentiating displacement with respect to time
at a fixed position.
In JEE, identify which velocity the question actually asks for before touching
a formula.
Why does a tighter rope transmit a disturbance faster?
Tension supplies the restoring influence that pulls neighboring parts into
motion.
Greater mass per unit length means more inertia.
For small transverse waves on an ideal uniform string, speed is the square root
of tension divided by mass per unit length.
We use mu for that linear mass density, measured in kilograms per meter.
Do not substitute volume density here.
Suppose a two meter string has mass four grams and tension eight newtons.
Convert four grams to zero point zero zero four kilograms.
Divide by two meters: mu is zero point zero zero two kilograms per meter.
The wave speed is the square root of four thousand, about sixty three point two
meters per second.
If tension becomes four times larger while mu stays fixed, predict the new
speed.
Pause for a moment.
The square root makes the speed twice as large.
Now imagine changing only the driving frequency.
With the same string and tension, wave speed remains the same in this ideal
model.
Since speed equals frequency times wavelength, doubling frequency halves
wavelength.
That's a very useful consistency check.
On a different medium the wavelength may change, but a wave transmitted across
a stationary boundary retains the driving frequency.
The particles and restoring forces determine the propagation speed; the source
sets the frequency.
Two pulses meet on a rope.
Do they collide like two solid objects?
In the linear wave model, no.
Their displacements add while they overlap, and then the pulses continue.
That is superposition.
Add signed displacements at the same position and time, not just the positive
heights drawn on a page.
A displacement of three centimeters upward combined with two centimeters
downward gives one centimeter upward.
For two coherent sinusoidal waves of the same frequency, with equal amplitude A
and constant phase difference, the resultant amplitude is twice A times the
absolute value of cosine of half the phase difference.
In phase, they reinforce; opposite in phase, they cancel.
With each amplitude two centimeters and a phase difference of one hundred and
twenty degrees, the resultant amplitude is two centimeters, not four.
Here cancellation means a local resultant displacement pattern; it does not
mean energy simply disappears from the entire wave system.
Now reflect a pulse from an ideal fixed end of a string.
The end cannot move, so the reflected displacement pulse is inverted.
At an ideal free end it reflects without displacement inversion.
These statements concern transverse string displacement, not a universal rule
for every pressure wave or boundary.
Incident and reflected waves can repeatedly overlap.
If their frequency, amplitude and boundary conditions match appropriately, that
overlap creates the standing patterns we'll study next.
Combine two identical sinusoidal waves traveling in opposite directions.
Their sum can be written as twice A times sine of k x times cosine of omega
t, after choosing a suitable phase origin.
Notice the separation: position determines the local amplitude, while time
makes each point oscillate.
The pattern doesn't march along the string.
Nodes stay at zero displacement; antinodes have the greatest amplitude.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, and a node to its nearest antinode
is a quarter wavelength.
For a string fixed at both ends, both ends must be nodes.
Its length must fit an integer number of half wavelengths.
That gives wavelength two L divided by n, and frequency n times wave speed
divided by two L.
The first harmonic is the fundamental.
On this string the second harmonic is the first overtone, and the third
harmonic is the second overtone.
Let's use length one meter and speed one hundred meters per second.
The fundamental is fifty hertz.
At the third harmonic, frequency is one hundred and fifty hertz and wavelength
is two thirds of a meter.
There are three loops, four nodes including the endpoints, and three antinodes.
Don't count loops as nodes.
An ideal standing wave formed by equal opposite traveling waves has no net time
averaged energy transport along the string, unlike either traveling wave on its
own.
Let's move from a string to air in a pipe.
Sound is longitudinal.
An ideal open end is a displacement antinode and approximately a pressure node.
A closed end is a displacement node and a pressure antinode.
Keep the quantity straight: pressure and displacement have opposite node
patterns.
Ignoring end correction, an open pipe at both ends fits half wavelengths and
has all integer harmonics.
A pipe closed at one end and open at the other fits an odd number of quarter
wavelengths, so only odd harmonics occur.
Its first overtone is the third harmonic, not the second.
For length half a meter and sound speed three hundred and forty meters per
second, a closed open pipe has fundamental one hundred and seventy hertz.
Its first overtone is five hundred and ten hertz.
Real open ends require an effective length correction, so use it if the
question supplies one.
Finally, hear two tones of two hundred and fifty six and two hundred and sixty
hertz together.
Their relative phase changes slowly, causing alternating reinforcement and
weakening.
You hear four beats per second: the absolute frequency difference.
Beats are easiest to notice for nearby frequencies and comparable amplitudes.
Unequal amplitudes need not produce complete silence at the minima.
To solve JEE wave problems, first name the wave quantity and boundary
conditions, then choose the relation.
A correct picture prevents far more errors than a longer formula list.
